body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod SafeParse result (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed credential. That wrapper object is then written as `key`, which corrupts the stored Google credential: on the next load `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails. Use `.data`, like the other call sites do. There is a second problem: this validates the merged `googleCredentials` rather than the token response. In sync mode the minimum schema strips `refresh_token`/`scope`/`token_type`, and then the placeholder `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` gets persisted.

When sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response`, not a gaxios response. `res?.data` is therefore undefined and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The fetch result has to be `await res.json()`'d, and the non-sync branch should return the same shape. The same shape mismatch affects hubspot, zohocrm, zoho-bigin, and any other caller that doesn't use fetch.

This schema doesn't do what the comments say. `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the literal string "[object Object]", so both computed keys resolve to the same property name and the second one overwrites the first. The effective schema is `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]"?: unknown }`. `z.object` also strips unknown keys by default, so `expires_in`/`expiry_date`/`refresh_token` returned by the sync endpoint are all dropped. For example, zoom then computes `expiry_date` from `undefined` (NaN), and office365 loses its expiry. Use `.passthrough()` or `z.record`/`catchall` instead.

This writes the literal string "refresh_token" as the refresh token whenever the response doesn't include one, even when sync is disabled. Many providers omit `refresh_token` on refresh; Microsoft's is optional in `refreshTokenResponseSchema`. office365calendar spreads `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credentials, so the real refresh token gets replaced by "refresh_token" and the next refresh fails permanently. Zoom does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` in sync mode, which has the same effect. Don't fabricate a value; keep the existing token.

The request to the self-hoster's sync endpoint carries no authentication: no webhook secret or header, and no signature. The endpoint returns live access tokens for any `calcomUserId`, so it has no way to verify the caller is Cal.com, and implementers are likely to leave it open. Send `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` in the configured header, or document the requirement. There is also no `response.ok` check and no Content-Type, so errors surface confusingly downstream.

This passes `credentialId` where `refreshOAuthTokens` expects the user id. The sync endpoint then receives the credential id as `calcomUserId` and returns (or fails to find) tokens for the wrong user. It should be `credential.userId`.

The Zoom app's slug is "zoom" (see `zoomvideo/_metadata.ts`), not "zoomvideo". The sync endpoint receives a slug that doesn't match what the webhook stores (it keys by `appStoreMetadata` slug), so the lookup fails.

This now does a token refresh on every `getClient` call, i.e. on every CalendarService construction, whether or not the token is expired. It also calls Salesforce directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so the new credential-sync path is never used for Salesforce. Separately, `response.statusText !== "OK"` is brittle: HTTP/2 responses have an empty statusText. Use `response.ok`.

The refreshed access token is saved to the DB, but the jsforce Connection is still built from the stale `credentialKey.access_token`/`instance_url`, so the refresh has no effect for this connection. Also, the refresh overwrites the stored key with only the schema fields. `z.object` strips anything else (for example `id_token`), and the key becomes `{...data, refresh_token}`, dropping the other previously stored fields.
Compare the secret with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`; `!==` on a string is not constant-time. Also, the header value can be a `string[]`, which would always fail the comparison.

`.parse` throws on an invalid body, and `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` below throw on a bad key or ciphertext. With no try/catch, client errors come back as unhandled 500s. Use `safeParse` and return 400. The decrypted keys are also stored with no validation against the app's key schema, and `req.method` isn't checked, although only POST should be accepted.

This matches the credential only by `userId` + `appId`, so if the user has multiple credentials for the same app (e.g. several Google accounts), an arbitrary one gets overwritten. Team credentials aren't supported either. It also doesn't check that the app is enabled before creating the credential.

`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` evaluates to a string or undefined, not a boolean; wrap it with `!!`. The sync endpoint isn't part of this flag, so every call site re-checks `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` separately. Consider adding a dedicated constant for it.

In sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch `Response`, but it's typed and used as a `HubspotToken`. `expiresIn` is undefined, so `expiryDate` becomes NaN, the Response object is persisted as the credential key, and `setAccessToken(undefined)` is called. The response needs to be parsed and normalized. zohocrm (`zohoCrmTokenInfo.data`) and zoho-bigin (`tokenInfo.data`) break the same way because they expect axios responses.
